study.title: Acts 10 - The Gospel Opening to Gentiles
study.overview: This chapter tells a decisive moment in Acts: God leads, through visions and action of the Holy Spirit, the encounter between Cornelius, a God-fearing Roman officer, and Peter, Jewish apostle. The central theme is not only the conversion of Cornelius, but the revelation that God does not treat people with favoritism and that the gospel of Jesus Christ also reaches the Gentiles. The account shows that the initiative is from God from beginning to end: he guides Cornelius, prepares Peter, gathers the witnesses, confirms the message with the Spirit and commands to baptize those who believed.

outline.title: Cornelius receives divine direction
outline.explanation: Cornelius, a centurion at Caesarea, is presented as a devout man, God-fearing, generous and persevering in prayer. An angel commands him to send men to Joppa to call Peter. Cornelius' immediate response shows obedience to the revelation received, and his home participates in this posture of sincere search for God.

outline.title: Peter gets the vision and accepts go
outline.explanation: As the envoys walk, Peter is also prepared by a vision in which animals considered unclean appear before him. The divine command corrects Peter's resistance to approach Gentiles. When the messengers arrive, the Spirit confirms that he must go without hesitation, and Peter hosts them, already initiating a practical breach of the barrier between Jews and Gentiles.

outline.title: The meeting in Caesarea and the common search for the word
outline.explanation: Cornelius gathers close relatives and friends to hear Peter, demonstrating serious expectation before God. Peter refuses any undue reverence and declares that God has shown him not to call anyone unclean. Cornelius then reports his vision and states that everyone is there to hear all that God has commanded. The focus becomes the word of God, not the social position of anyone.

outline.title: The gospel, the Spirit, and the baptism of the Gentiles
outline.explanation: Peter announces that God makes no sense of people and summarizes the work of Jesus: anointing, ministry of power, death, resurrection and commission for testimony and forgiveness of sins. As he speaks, the Holy Spirit falls on the Gentile listeners, causing admiration in the Jewish believers present. The conclusion is their baptism in the name of the Lord, followed by Peter's stay with that group for a few days.

study.context: Acts 10 is set in Caesarea and Joppa, two cities mentioned in the text itself. The chapter shows the transition from the proclamation of the gospel predominantly among Jews to its explicit reception among Gentiles. The text also highlights Jewish customs of ritual and social separation, which Peter recognizes, but that God redefines in the light of purification granted by himself. It is not necessary to go beyond the chapter to realize that this episode marks a central advance in the expansion of the church.
study.theology: The chapter teaches that salvation does not depend on ethnicity, social status or belonging prior to Judaism, but on God's graceful initiative in Christ. Cornelius' prayers and alms do not buy salvation, but they show a man already sensitive to God and ready to receive the message. Peter's vision not only deals with food, but also about the removal of the separation that prevented the communion between Jews and Gentiles. Peter's sermon concentrates the gospel on Jesus: his public life, his death, his resurrection, and his authority as Judge of the living and the dead. The outpouring of the Holy Spirit before baptism confirms that God welcomes the Gentiles in the same family of faith. The chapter therefore unites an implicit repentance, faith, gift of the Spirit and baptism as signs of the entry of these new believers into the Christian community.

scholarViews.insight: The commentary highlights that Luke shows, already in Cornelius, that Christianity was not hostile to the Roman authorities and that this officer appears as a Gentile open to the gospel of peace in Jesus Christ.

The note points out that here the door of faith opens to the Gentiles and that Peter is the first to admit uncircumcised in the Christian church, making this chapter a new and surprising milestone in the history of Acts.
The commentator notes that Cornelius was a devout man who taught his home to fear God and practiced generosity, showing that his piety was expressed in prayer and beneficence.

questions: What attitudes of Cornelius show that he was really seeking God, and not just being religious?
What does Peter's vision teach about spiritual prejudices and barriers of coexistence between peoples?
How does the chapter help to understand that the Holy Spirit confirms the inclusion of the Gentiles in God's family?
study.practice: Today, this chapter calls the reader to abandon any idea of spiritual or social superiority before other people. The concrete practice is to receive Peter's same posture: to hear the voice of God, to break unjust barriers, to welcome those who Christ welcomes and to proclaim the gospel with clarity. He also teaches us to value the meeting of the house: Cornelius calls relatives and friends to hear the word, and this challenges the believer to use his home as a space for listening, prayer and witness.
study.uncertainty: The biblical text does not inform the exact date or historical details outside the account itself; therefore, any broader reconstruction of the Roman or Jewish context must remain cautious. Nor can it be affirmed, only on the basis of this chapter, that Cornelius' prayers and alms saved him before the gospel; the text itself presents these practices as signs of his openness to God and that he would be led to the message of Christ. The confessional interpretations of the exact meaning of the view of animals or the relationship between baptism and the reception of the Spirit should be read as theological readings, not as indisputable conclusions of the text.
